opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons. The first is simply that every time we push the frontier, we find that the models become capable of things that weren't possible before. These aren't just incremental improvements on the same tasks; new capabilities emerge that open up entirely new applications. Things like being able to reason through a multi-step problem, write and debug substantial pieces of code, or understand video and audio together with text. Each of those unlocks real value for people.

The second reason is that the frontier models are what let you build everything else. Once you have a very capable large model, you can distill it into smaller, more efficient models that run cheaply and quickly, on a phone or at huge scale. So pushing the top end actually raises the quality of the whole family of models that people use day to day. If you don't have a great frontier model, your smaller models aren't going to be as good either.

And third, and probably most important to me personally, is the potential impact on really hard problems. Areas like healthcare, scientific discovery, education, and making information accessible to people in their own language. I think we're at the point where these models can be genuine collaborators for scientists and engineers, helping people explore ideas faster and tackle problems that would otherwise take years. That's tremendously exciting.

There's also just the intellectual side of it. We still don't fully understand why these systems work as well as they do, or what the right architectures and training approaches will look like in five years. There's a lot of headroom left in algorithms, in hardware co-design, in efficiency. So building at the frontier is how you keep learning, and how you make sure that progress happens in a thoughtful and responsible way.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier progress reveals new capabilities that were not possible before, giving examples such as multi-step reasoning and understanding video and audio with text.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I'm still curious, and the problems are still interesting, and they keep getting more interesting rather than less. When I started at Google, the problems were things like how do you index the whole web and serve a query in a couple hundred milliseconds. Those were great problems. But what we're working on now is really different in kind. We're building systems that can read, write, reason, look at images, write code, help a biologist design an experiment. The surface area of what these models can touch is enormous.

And I think there's a real argument that capability matters here, that it's not just a score on a benchmark. When a model goes from getting a hard math problem right thirty percent of the time to ninety percent of the time, that's the difference between a toy and something a researcher will actually lean on. The same is true for medical imaging, or for understanding a codebase, or for helping someone who doesn't speak English well access information. The frontier is where you find out what's possible, and a lot of the applications that end up mattering the most weren't obvious until the capability was there.

There's also a systems side to this that I find really fun personally. Training these models is one of the biggest engineering problems anyone has ever worked on. You're thinking about chip design, interconnects, how you partition computation across tens of thousands of accelerators, how you keep that running reliably for weeks. Every generation, the constraints change, and you get to rethink the whole stack. I like that. That's the part that gets me out of bed.

And then I'd say we want to do it responsibly. Pushing the frontier isn't separate from understanding these systems. A lot of the work on safety, on evaluation, on efficiency, happens because you're close to the most capable models and you can see what they do and don't do. I'd rather we be in that position, learning carefully, than not. So the short answer is: the problems are compelling, the potential benefit is large, and I still think we've only scratched the surface of what these systems can do for people.

r001.rationale: The response says the frontier reveals what is possible and that important applications often become apparent only after models gain the needed capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that we’re still a long way from systems that can help with all the things we’d like them to help with. You look at scientific research, or education, or healthcare, and there are so many places where better AI could make a real difference.

One thing I find particularly exciting is helping scientists explore ideas much faster. If you can shorten the time between having a hypothesis and figuring out whether it’s promising, you can accelerate discovery across a lot of different fields.

And pushing the frontier isn’t just about making a bigger model. It’s about making models more capable, more reliable, and more efficient, so those capabilities are useful to more people. There are still a lot of hard research problems there. That combination of interesting technical challenges and the potential to help people is what keeps me excited.

r001.rationale: The response describes broader usefulness, scientific progress, and making models more capable, reliable, and efficient, but does not identify discovering capabilities missing from earlier, less capable models as a reason to build frontier models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the motivation is that we’re still a long way from systems that can help with the full range of things people want to do. You can see these models becoming useful for writing code, learning something new, or making sense of complicated information, but you can also see where they fall short. They make mistakes. They struggle with tasks that require sustained reasoning.

Pushing the frontier is about expanding what’s possible. If we can build systems that help scientists explore more ideas, or give people access to expertise they wouldn’t otherwise have, that’s tremendously valuable. The research is fascinating, but what really motivates me is turning those advances into something useful for people.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier work is about “expanding what’s possible,” but does not identify discovering capabilities absent from earlier, less capable models.
